name: Biblically-Attested Minor Levantine Deities
note: Hub collective for the DDD set of minor Northwest-Semitic gods named (mostly polemically) in the Hebrew Bible — the foreign gods of Samaria's resettled peoples (2 Kings 17) and Philistine/Sidonian local cults; grouping entity, not a worshipped deity.

name: Baal-Zebub of Ekron
note: Philistine city-god of Ekron consulted as a healing oracle by King Ahaziah (2 Kings 1). Name = 'Lord of the Flies', almost certainly a Hebrew polemical distortion of an original Baal epithet ('zbl/Zebul' = 'Prince', as at Ugarit). The ORIGINAL deity behind the later Christian demon Beelzebub. Homonym note: distinct from the demon Beelzebul (ENT_CHR_BEELZEBUL), which is his reception.

name: Ashima of Hamath
note: Deity of the people of Hamath, named among the gods made by Samaria's resettled peoples (2 Kings 17:30). Plausibly connected to a NW-Semitic goddess Asham/Ashima attested at Elephantine (Anat-Ashima) and possibly to the Aramaean cult of Hamath; later rabbinic tradition imagined her as a goat/bald-figure idol.

name: Adrammelech
note: God of Sepharvaim to whom child sacrifice ('passing through fire') was made (2 Kings 17:31). Name = 'Adad/Adar is king' or 'the king is exalted'; identity debated — linked variously to Adad, a solar/Molek-type cult, or an Aramaean/Assyrian deity. Paired with Anammelech.

name: Anammelech
note: God of Sepharvaim receiving child sacrifice alongside Adrammelech (2 Kings 17:31). Name = 'Anu/Anath is king'; proposed links to the Mesopotamian sky-god Anu, a lunar deity, or (via 'Anath-melek') the Canaanite goddess Anat. Identity uncertain.

name: Nibhaz
note: God of the Avvites, named with Tartak among Samaria's resettled gods (2 Kings 17:31). Etymology obscure and possibly a scribal corruption; later Jewish tradition fancifully described a dog-shaped idol. No independent epigraphic attestation.

name: Tartak
note: God of the Avvites, paired with Nibhaz (2 Kings 17:31). Etymology uncertain (possibly an Elamite/Iranian theonym or scribal corruption); rabbinic tradition imagined an ass-shaped idol. No independent attestation outside the biblical notice.

name: Astronoe
note: Sidonian goddess known from Damascius (Life of Isidore): a mountain-mother/huntress who, on the youth Eshmun's self-mutilation, revives and deifies him. Generally read as a hellenized aspect of Astarte tied to the Eshmun healing cult at Sidon.
